scenarios.name: single filer, age 55 (below 62), survivor of a DC/federal government annuitant: fails DC's age gate, correctly fully taxable -- contrast/regression case
scenarios.source: D.C. Code Section 47-1803.02(a)(2)(N)(ii): 'Survivor benefits received from the District of Columbia or the federal government by persons who are 62 years of age or older by the end of the taxable year' are excluded from DC gross income. At age 55, this taxpayer fails the age-62 gate, so the survivor benefit is fully taxable. Arithmetic: $50,000 - $14,600 single standard deduction = $35,400 taxable. DC brackets: 4% to $10,000 ($400.00), 6% on the remaining $25,400 ($1,524.00). Total $1,924.00.

scenarios.name: single filer, age 65 (62+), survivor of a DC/federal government annuitant: fully exempt, uncapped, engine taxes it in full
scenarios.source: D.C. Code Section 47-1803.02(a)(2)(N)(ii) (see above; no dollar cap and no sunset clause on this subparagraph, unlike (N)(i) below). Confirmed by DC OTR's 2024 D-40 Booklet, page 17, Schedule I 'Subtractions from DC Income', 'Line 12 DC and federal government survivor benefits': 'If you are an annuitant's survivor and 62 years of age or older as of December 31, 2024, enter the total survivor benefits (do not include Social Security survivor benefits).' The District's own government pension is labelled 'ownStateOrLocal' here: the taxpayer's OWN jurisdiction's public retirement system, which is what the District government is to a DC resident. Phase 5b Task 1 added that PlanSource case and Task 2 re-labelled this row onto it. It previously read 'otherStateOrLocal', disclosed at the time as 'the closest available generic' label; that was not merely imprecise, because 'otherStateOrLocal' means a DIFFERENT jurisdiction's system, so a DC rule written against it would have exempted a Maryland state pension held by a DC resident, which D.C. Code Section 47-1803.02(a)(2)(N)(ii) does not. The survivor-versus-own distinction is now a STRUCTURED field too, not only prose: 'isSurvivorBenefit': true on the row below. Task 1 added the flag to the production type RetirementPlanClassification and Task 2 added it to this fixture schema (ClassifiedPensionSource), after measuring that the schema silently DISCARDED the key before that -- a fixture setting it decoded and re-encoded with the key simply gone, no error raised. It matters because this file's DC-2/DC-3/DC-4 (survivor) and DC-5 (own pension) share the (planSource: federalCivilian, planStructure: definedBenefit) pair for contradictory required treatment, and every party in those cases is 62 or older, so age cannot separate them either (see DC-3/DC-4's knownDefect entries and the phase ledger's Bucket 4 for the full discussion). Nothing CONSUMES the flag yet: wiring it into PerSourceExemptionRule matching is Task 9's work, so this fixture's pinned figures are unmoved by carrying it. Arithmetic: $50,000 fully excluded, $0 taxable, tax = $0.00.

knownDefect.summary: DC/federal government survivor benefits are fully excluded at age 62+ with no cap (D.C. Code 47-1803.02(a)(2)(N)(ii)); statetax-2026-DC.json has no perSourceExemptions, so the engine taxes the full $50,000.

scenarios.name: MFJ, both spouses 62+, both survivors of DC/federal government annuitants (stipulated): fully exempt, engine taxes the full household income
scenarios.source: D.C. Code Section 47-1803.02(a)(2)(N)(ii) (see above). Arithmetic: $30,000 + $25,000 = $55,000, all fully excluded, $0 taxable after the $25,900 MFJ standard deduction, tax = $0.00.

FORMER CANNOT_VERIFY, NOW RESOLVED: DC-3/DC-4 (survivor benefit) require full exemption for (planSource: federalCivilian, planStructure: definedBenefit), while DC-5 (own pension, same pair) requires that pair fully taxable, and both parties are 62 or older in every case, so age cannot separate them either. Phase 5b Task 1 added isSurvivorBenefit to the production type RetirementPlanClassification and Task 2 added it to this fixture's schema and set it on every survivor row here, so the two treatments now sit on distinguishable data and this file IS satisfiable. scenarios.name: MFJ, one spouse (65) is a DC/federal survivor and exempt, the other spouse (60) has a taxable private pension: one spouse qualifies
scenarios.source: D.C. Code Section 47-1803.02(a)(2)(N)(ii) (survivor benefit, DC/federal government only). Arithmetic: $30,000 survivor benefit fully excluded; $60,000 private pension fully taxable. DC AGI = $90,000 - $30,000 = $60,000; taxable = $60,000 - $25,900 MFJ standard deduction = $34,100. DC brackets: 4% to $10,000 ($400.00), 6% on the next $24,100 ($1,446.00). Total $1,846.00.

scenarios.name: single filer, age 65, OWN federal civil service pension (not a survivor benefit): the general $3,000 pension exclusion EXPIRED in 2015 -- correctly fully taxable, engine also taxes it fully -- MATCH, correcting an assumption in this batch's own brief
scenarios.source: D.C. Code Section 47-1803.02(a)(2)(N)(i): 'Pension, military retired pay, or annuity income received from the District of Columbia or the federal government by persons who are 62 years of age or older...except that the exclusion shall not exceed the lesser of $3,000...provided further, that this sub-subparagraph shall apply for taxable years beginning before January 1, 2015.' Confirmed by DC OTR's 2024 D-40 Booklet (all 97 pages searched): no pension-exclusion line exists anywhere in the current Schedule I subtractions list; only 'Line 12 DC and federal government survivor benefits' (subparagraph (N)(ii), which has no sunset clause) remains. This app's Task 7 brief describes DC's rule as '$3,000 at 62 or over, DC or federal government pensions only' -- that description is the EXPIRED (N)(i) provision; current law for a LIVING retiree's own pension grants no DC exclusion at all. Arithmetic: $50,000 - $14,600 standard deduction = $35,400 taxable, same DC-bracket math as the age-55 case above. Tax = $1,924.00, and the engine already agrees, since it also grants no pension exclusion.
